It is near-silent (about a fifth of the corpus base rate) on articles, copulas, spatial prepositions and inanimate or first-person-plural pronouns (the, a, is, are, in, on, at, with, it, this, that, which, we, us, our, my); outside that class its strongest peaks fall on a few concrete-noun onsets (customer, phone, car, cat, gun), which fire on the token itself wherever it appears.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Lighthouse keeping began as a lonely trade, and the men who took the job often stayed on remote rocks for months at a time. Their duties were simple on paper: trim the wick, polish the lens, wind the clockwork, and keep a steady watch through the night. In practice the work demanded a patience that few could sustain. Storms would cut the station off for weeks, and the keeper had to ration oil, flour, and fresh water with an attention that bordered on obsession.

The great lamps of the nineteenth century were marvels of engineering. Fresnel lenses, ground from hundreds of glass prisms, could throw a beam more than twenty miles out to sea. Each lens weighed several tons and floated on a bath of mercury so that it might turn with almost no friction. Keepers learned to read the weather by the colour of the horizon, and they kept journals in which every change was recorded with a care that seems, to a modern reader, almost religious.

Life at the station followed a rhythm of its own. The keeper rose before dawn, lit the lamp if the night watch had not already done so, and swept the tower stairs. Breakfast was usually porridge, tea, and whatever bread the last supply boat had brought. Visitors were rare, and a passing ship might signal with flags or a lantern to ask for news. The keeper would answer by hoisting a code of his own, and the exchange of signals, brief as it was, could carry a man through a difficult week. A keeper might spend her whole career at one light, and her name would never appear in the record.

By the middle of the twentieth century the trade had begun to disappear. Automation arrived first on the smaller stations, where a gas accumulator and a sun valve could do the work of a man. Larger lights followed, and by the 1980s most keepers had been withdrawn. Some stayed on as attendants, visiting the tower every few months to change the lamp and test the fog signal, but the old discipline of the night watch was gone.

Historians of technology like to point out that the lighthouse is a rare case of a monument built for a single purpose and then rendered obsolete by a device that does the same job without a keeper. The towers remain, of course, repainted and opened to tourists, and all of them are now maintained by a national trust, and on a clear evening the beam still sweeps the water at intervals of ten seconds. Anyone who has stood on the gallery in a rising wind will tell you that the romance of the place survives the machinery. The light is automatic now, and yet it still turns, and the sea still takes the same toll of ships that it took a hundred years ago.

What the keepers left behind is mostly paper: logbooks, letters, inventories, and a great many rules about the storage of oil. These records are the raw material of a small but stubborn branch of social history, and they repay reading. A logbook entry from a storm in 1883 records that the keeper could not leave the tower for nine days, and that his lamp burned without interruption while the sea broke over the gallery rail. Historians who have worked through these volumes agree that the handwriting is steady even on the worst nights, a detail that says more about the discipline of the trade than any official report.
